newsitem.title: JORDAN: Budding world leaders seek tips for the top.
newsitem.headline: Budding world leaders seek tips for the top.

text.p: Aspiring world leaders of the 21st century gathered in Jordan on Sunday for a United Nations workshop aimed at grooming them for future power.

The 160 budding politicians, tycoons and visionaries from around the globe met at the inaugural session of the U.N. International Leadership Academy, a month-long training programme offering tips for life at the top.
"This institution is aimed exclusively at training for leadership at a global level," said Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul-Salam al-Majali, who campaigned for years for the academy's establishment.
"It shows our commitment to a generation of forward-looking leaders here in the region and in the world," he said.
Delegates picked for the workship include an airline ticket agent from Uganda, a Malaysian metaphysical philosopher and an employee at the library of former U.S. President Richard Nixon.
Over the next four weeks they will glean tips on leadership from prime ministers, ministers, diplomats and academics.

Norwegian Foreign Minister Jan Egeland will speak on his country's peace-making efforts in the Middle East and the Balkans and former Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres will speak on leadership and peace in the Middle East.
U.N. Under-Secretary General Nafis Sadik and senior figures in U.N. truce monitoring and political affairs will discuss "The United Nations and the Challenge of Global Leadership".
Organisers hope the academy will forge a group of future leaders with a broad agenda to tackle global poverty, promote peace and equality, and protect the environment.

"This challenging new venture is designed to create a community of potential future leaders who have shared a common training experience in global issues," said Heitor Gurgulino de Souza, rector of the United Nations University.
Jordan's Queen Noor said the gathering was devoted to instilling an "appreciation of the interrelated nature of today's global challenges in emerging world leaders."
She said it should help promote a "new kind of leadership, more comprehensive in its approach to problem-solving."
President of the World Academy of Arts and Sciences Harlan Cleveland said the spread of technology and information meant that power would have to be exercised very differently in the next century.

"The rapid globalisation of ideas and markets will require new policies and international agreements for governance and business," he said. "In our communities, our nations, and our world, nobody can possible be in general charge -- of anything."
